## Your goal

To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## What carries over

This session starts with no memory of the earlier ones: your conversation is not carried over. Your working directory does carry over: every file in it stays as you leave it. If AGENTS.md exists there, it is loaded into your context at the start of every session (its first 64 KiB); your other files are there to read with the file tools. ## This game

A new game. You play Black, so you move first.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll stay with 20k for game 43, review the latest two games, and focus on broad territory with a concrete two-eye plan before enclosure. I’ll save the full game and update the lessons afterward.

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi7, simple ko.

## Area expansion did not establish life

Against E5/G7/E3, C3/G3 established lower bases and C5/G5 broadened both sides.
D3 joined C3 before pressure at E4. C6/B6 expanded the upper-left boundary.
C4 joined the left chains; G4 joined the right chains.
These prompt connections were useful, but connected stones did not prove two eyes.

At move10, the provisional side targets were A/B/C rows1–5=15 and G/H/J rows1–5=15.
Even hoped-for D/F rows1–3 gave only36, below White38 at a complete81-point split.
The D/F points were particularly conditional beside Black E3.
Later left A/B/C rows1–6 plus D1–D3=21 and right G/H/J rows1–6=18 gave conditional39.
That count was slim and omitted the effect of competing closure and eye-making turns.

G6/H6 expanded the right upward.
D2/D1 secured the lower-left first line, but Black J6 took one right point during those turns.
J5 ataried J6 solelyJ7; Black J7 connected it, and H5 promptly joined J5.

No B4/A4 or other divider was played, so do not describe two completed eyes on the final board.

F3 expanded by one point beyond right17.
Black F2 followed, then White G2, Black G1, White H2, Black H1.
G1/H1 removed two lower points: 17+1−2=16, making left21+right16=37 even if both survived.
D4/F4 were possible additional shared-boundary points, but Black D4 later took one, and neither could supply an eye merely by being filled.
More importantly, the G1/H1 undercut removed the right group's lower eye boundary.
Earlier G2/G1, a wider base, or a different orientation require fresh reading; none is established as a winning replacement.
Do not repeat the full C3/G3/C5/G5 lower-side plan blindly.

## Right capture left only one two-point eye

After H2, direct J1 would start with onlyJ2 because H1 was Black.
J2 at40 instead joined H2. Black J3 entered the remaining room with H3/J4 liberties.

J4 boundaries: H4/J3/J5.

F4 touches Black E4/F5; J1 touches Black H1.

H2/H3/H4 added joined stones and contained the invasion, but consumed the room that had been counted as potential eye space.

E8 at46 attempted the open upper band rather than spending more stones inside the failed right group.
F8/G8/H8 broadened connected upper stones.
Black D7 connected all Black groups; D8 and E9 then constrained the upper-left end.

White D9 would have onlyC9, and Black C9 captures it and reopens D9 for E9.
This is the same capture-opening issue as game41's C9 sacrifice.

J8 at56 joined H8 and closed a potential G9/H9/J9 straight-three space.
White would need H9 next to divide it into trueG9 and trueJ9.
Black immediately played H9 at57, occupying the divider.
I explicitly considered that reply before J8; playing J8 anyway did not make the second turn available.

Final upper six: E8/F8/F9/G8/H8/J8.
Liberties: E7/G9/J9.
G9/J9 are shared with opposing Black H9, not true White eyes.
E7 reaches E6, but both touch the main Black boundary.

Limited manual line from the final board:
W G9, B E7, W J9 captures H9, B H9 captures all eight upper White stones.
White J9 is legal because capturing H9 opens H9; the whole eight-stone White group then has soleH9.
No ko: White J9 joins a larger group, and Black H9 captures eight.
The symmetric W J9, B E7, W G9, B H9 also captures eight.
Capturing the divider consumes G9/J9 and leaves just one trueH9 eye, rather than the original pair.
This is the same warning as games36–37 and game40's G8-divider correction.
No outside rescue or exhaustive death proof is claimed.

With both right and upper groups lacking a second eye and no viable coordinated capture identified, I resigned.
There is no official numerical score and no fabricated dead-stone area count.

## Carry forward

1. Retain20k: nine wins, twenty-seven losses, two draws.
2. Count life-making turns as part of the plan. Conditional39 was too slim, and G1/H1 undermined both area and right life.
3. Secure lower eye boundaries while available. F3 was a real one-point expansion, but the subsequent F2/G1/H1 sequence had a larger cost; an earlier alternative still needs manual reading.
4. J3/J4 is one two-point region. Capturing two stones does not establish two eyes.
5. Inventory changes must change the plan before enclosure: after H4/F1, the right group had only one enclosed space, regardless of its thirteen connected stones.
6. Inspect opponent divider replies and act on them. J8 followed by Black H9 was anticipated but still allowed; naming the problem was not enough.
7. Capture openings must be rebuilt. Upper H9 capture opens one eye and allows immediate large-group capture after E7 closes the outside liberty.
8. Preserve useful joins C4/G4/H5/D2/D1, but do not confuse them with life or added territory.
9. Replay matched30 boards/captures and all57 moves are saved; no numerical resignation score, optimal opening or verified winning replacement is claimed.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
Detailed historical lessons7–116 are archived verbatim in go-lessons-games-002-through-028.md. Read the relevant review or archive when a familiar tactical pattern matters.

117. Game29 retained all Black stones and drew44–37+7. The early37 then35 selected outline was too small; expansion reached48 conditionally, but competing endpoint reductions left44. 119. Game29 C1/A3 supplied true C2/A4 before any left capture. A1 then captured BOTH A2/B1; isolated A1 and the main group share true A2/B1 with boundaries A1/A3/B2 and A1/B2/C1. J8 captured H8; isolated J8 and the right main group share true H8/J9 with boundaries G8/H7/H9/J8 and H9/J8. Each boundary group retains the other eye on either enemy fill; do not spend unnecessary connection turns.

These verified replies prevent a forced capture; no exhaustive attack claim. Central/lower share separate E6 and F4/F5 spaces; B E6 is suicide but B F4/F5 is legal and answered at the other point. ## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
Detailed historical lessons7–116 are archived verbatim in go-lessons-games-002-through-028.md. Read the relevant review or archive when a familiar tactical pattern matters.

## Development: three bases consumed competing turns

C3/C7 took the left against White F7/F4. G3 supplied a lower-right base.
White D4/C4 cut C3 from C5. B4 blocked the left edge, C6 joined C5/C7, and B3 joined C3/B4.
Those were actual useful joins, but B5 remained unplayed, so the two three-stone left groups were still separate at the end.
Their large empty left base remained open through C2/C8 and the upper center; no enclosed two-eye proof was completed.

At move10, A/B/C all rows except White C4 gave conditional26, plus hoped-for G/H/J rows1–6=18 gave44.
That was below Black45 and the right target had no established boundary.
G4 joined G3, but White G5 capped it immediately.
At16, left26 plus G/H/J rows1–4=12 gave only38, also conditional.
G7 at17 therefore changed the plan by establishing an upper-right base.
The count did trigger expansion, but the expansion created another vulnerable group with several competing life turns.
No particular opening replacement or individual move value is verified.
Do not count the unplayed left endpoints or right eye boundaries as retained area.

## Decisive upper error: a join left the whole group in atari

G7/H7 broadened upper-right; White G6/H6 shut its lower boundary.
G8/G9 retained the first line against F8/F9.
The upper group G7/G8/G9/H7 then had H8/H9/J7, not eyes.

J6 at25 tried to supply the missing J7 boundary.
It was isolated with J5/J7; it was not a completed eye divider or connection.
White J8 invaded with H8/J7/J9.
H8 at27 joined the upper group and left White J8 with J7/J9.
White J5 at28 put isolated J6 in atari at J7.

The exact pre-J7 inventory:
- Upper G7/G8/G9/H7/H8: H9/J7.
- Isolated J6: J7.
- White J8: J7/J9.

Black J7 joined the two Black groups and ataried White J8 at J9.
But it also consumed J7, leaving ALL SEVEN Black stones with sole H9.
White H9 at30 immediately captured G7/G8/G9/H7/H8/J6/J7.
White J8 survived and gained H8/J7 liberties after the capture.

My pre-move reasoning incorrectly expected a later Black J9 reply after White H9.
That reply did not exist because White H9 captured the whole boundary first.
The current-board inventory before J7 already contained the information needed to avoid this error.
A connection is unsafe when the union of both groups' liberties, after removing the joining point and accounting for captures, is a single opponent-playable liberty.
An atari against another enemy group does not prevent that enemy's capture of your own group.
Apply the allowed inspection to the exact proposed move when uncertain; do not inspect the current board and then override it with a narrative.

## Lower fight: undercut, isolated stone and actual ko

G2 at31 joined G3/G4, but White F2 extended its existing F3/F4 group.
H4 at33 broadened the joined lower-right boundary; White G1 undercut.
H1 at35 blocked further bottom extension and ataried G1 at F1.
G1 had BOTH F1/H1 beforehand; White F1 correctly connected it to F2/F3/F4.
Black H1 remained isolated with H2/J1.
J4 at37 joined H4 and closed the top of the lower-right room.

White H2 at38 left isolated Black H1 soleJ1.
The lower main G2/G3/G4/H4/J4 had H3/H5/J3.
White H2 had H3/J2.
Black J2 at39 ataried H2 at H3 but did not connect or save H1:
J2 was isolated with J1/J3, and H1 still had soleJ1.

White J1 at40 captured H1 and explicitly marked H1 as ko.
The capture also opened H1 for White H2 and the F1–G1 group.
Afterward Black J2 had soleJ3, White H2 had H1/H3, and White J1 had soleH1.
The original note saying H1 could recapture omitted that IMMEDIATE H1 was forbidden by simple ko.
Black J3 at41 joined J2 to J4 and saved that stone.
This was a necessary connection, not an effective ko threat.
White H1 at42 joined J1/H2/G1/F1–F4, permanently closing the lower boundary.
No recapture was attempted or refused.

## Final seven: opposing-color shared liberties, no eyes

Final lower Black G2/G3/G4/H4/J2/J3/J4 had exactly H3/H5.
H3 touches White H2; H5 touches White G5/H6/J5.
Neither is a Black eye or seki space.

Specified manual local lines from the final board:
- B H3, W H5 captures eight Black stones.
- B H5 ataries White J5 at J6, but W J6 joins J5 to H6 and leaves Black soleH3. Black H3 is suicide because it captures no White group; W H3 captures eight.
- White-first H3 leaves Black soleH5. Black H5 is suicide while White J5 retains J6; W H5 captures seven if Black plays elsewhere.

These are limited direct-extension lines, not exhaustive future search or proof against all remote threats.
White's connected lower group retains E1/E2/E3/E4/F5; the upper central White group retains several outside liberties.
No coordinated outside rescue was identified.
With the upper seven already lost and no two-eye plan for the remaining right seven, I resigned.
The left six were not physically captured and retained an unfinished open base.
No numerical resignation score is fabricated.

## Carry forward

1. Retain20k: nine wins, twenty-eight losses, two draws.
2. Before an urgent join, list the resulting complete group's liberties. Game43 J7 saved isolated J6 only by putting all seven stones in atari at H9.
3. Check whether the opponent's reply captures your boundary BEFORE reading a later capture of their invader. White H9 removed the group immediately; Black J9 was never available.
4. Current-position inventories must constrain the choice. The pre-J7 H9/J7 and J7 lists already refuted the intended move.
5. A conditional44 outline is below Black45 and is especially weak when it includes unplayed endpoints. Additional bases need enough time and room for two eyes.
6. H1-first left an isolated stone; J4 supplied another boundary, but H2 cut before H2/J2 division. Earlier move orders require fresh manual reading, not an asserted fix.
7. A capture reopens liberties for adjacent enemy groups: White J1 reopened H1 for H2/G1. Respect the explicit ko marker; a necessary connection is not automatically a ko threat.
8. Final H3/H5 were shared with White, not true Black eyes or seki. B H5's atari did not force a capture because White J6 connected.
9. Replay matched23 boards/captures and42 actual moves; save the failed reading and its correction without inferring move values from the result.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
Detailed historical lessons7–116 are archived verbatim in go-lessons-games-002-through-028.md. Read the relevant review or archive when a familiar tactical pattern matters.
